lesson.title: Flipping Tangent Upside Down
lesson.summary: Cotangent is the reciprocal of tangent, so the reciprocal rule turns the just derived derivative of tangent directly into the derivative of cotangent, giving negative csc squared x.
lesson.body:
Cotangent is the reciprocal of tangent, cot x = 1/tan x, and that relationship is the fastest route to its derivative now that d/dx tan x = sec^2 x has already been established. Rather than starting over with a fresh limit computation, the reciprocal rule can be applied directly to the function tan x, treating it as the g(x) inside a 1/g(x) expression.

Recall the reciprocal rule: d/dx [1/g(x)] = -g'(x)/[g(x)]^2. Let g(x) = tan x, so g'(x) = sec^2 x, the result just derived. Substituting gives d/dx cot x = -sec^2 x / tan^2 x. This can be simplified using the definitions sec x = 1/cos x and tan x = sin x/cos x: sec^2 x / tan^2 x = (1/cos^2 x) / (sin^2 x/cos^2 x) = 1/sin^2 x, which is csc^2 x. So the derivative simplifies to d/dx cot x = -csc^2 x.

It is reassuring that the quotient rule, applied directly to cot x = cos x / sin x instead of going through the reciprocal rule, gives the identical answer. With f(x) = cos x, f'(x) = -sin x, g(x) = sin x, g'(x) = cos x, the quotient rule gives [(-sin x)(sin x) - (cos x)(cos x)] / sin^2 x = [-sin^2 x - cos^2 x] / sin^2 x = -(sin^2 x + cos^2 x)/sin^2 x = -1/sin^2 x = -csc^2 x, matching exactly. Having two independent routes land on the same formula is a strong confirmation that -csc^2 x is correct.

A worked check at x = pi/4 illustrates the result. cot(pi/4) = 1, and the formula predicts a derivative of -csc^2(pi/4). Since sin(pi/4) = sqrt(2)/2, csc(pi/4) = 1/sin(pi/4) = sqrt(2), so csc^2(pi/4) = 2, giving a predicted derivative of -2. Using the earlier numerical estimate that tan(pi/4 + 0.001) is about 1.002003, cot(pi/4+0.001) = 1/1.002003, about 0.998001. The difference quotient [0.998001 - 1]/0.001 is about -1.999, matching -2 very closely.

Just as sec^2 x could never be negative and forced tan x to always climb, -csc^2 x can never be positive, since csc^2 x is a square, so the derivative of cotangent is always negative wherever cotangent is defined. This means cot x is decreasing across every interval between its vertical asymptotes, sliding continuously downward from positive infinity to negative infinity rather than ever leveling off, the mirror image of tangent's relentless climb. The domains of cotangent and its derivative also line up exactly: cot x = cos x/sin x is undefined wherever sin x = 0, at every integer multiple of pi, and csc^2 x = 1/sin^2 x is undefined at exactly those same points, since it too depends on dividing by sin x, a consistency worth checking whenever a reciprocal or quotient rule is applied.

The pattern connecting these last two results is worth remembering: cotangent's derivative is not a brand new fact to memorize from scratch, it is tangent's derivative run through the reciprocal rule you already covered. This same move, taking the reciprocal of a function whose derivative you know and applying the reciprocal rule, is about to reappear when secant and cosecant are related to cosine and sine in exactly the same way.
